extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of romance fiction; general literary-interested public
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for understanding and writing romances set in the Regency period (or Regency-set historical romances), including common tropes, stylistic expectations, and choices between traditional restraint and more modern/explicit approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common Regency romance tropes
rubrics_metrics.description: Some common tropes found in these stories include an anachronistically independent heroine who must contend with strict social rules, a Season packed with balls and dances, vicious gossip that spreads like wildfire, and a happily-ever-after with a reformed rake of a duke (or viscount).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These recurring elements (heroine vs. social constraint, social Season events, gossip as plot engine, reformed-rake HEA) are hallmark devices to deploy when crafting a Regency-set romance; examples include popular modern adaptations such as Bridgerton.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional Regency characteristics (style and social focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Sparkling dialogue; intelligent, well-turned phrases; a glittering, though highly restrictive, social backdrop; and a preoccupation with the importance of social consequence and behavior."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phrasing (from librarians Neal Wyatt et al.) defines the 'traditional Regency' aesthetic: prioritize witty, polished dialogue and place social rules and consequences at the center of conflict and characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meticulous historical research and narrow class focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Georgette Heyer wrote over two dozen meticulously researched historical books, all set in Jane Austen’s era, with an obsessive focus on London’s tiny upper class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emulate Heyer’s model by researching period detail and concentrating on the nuanced behaviors, fashions, and institutions of the Regency-era upper class to create authenticity and texture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralize female subjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Heyer’s popularity 'helped transform historical fiction into a more feminine space that continues to centralise female subjectivity, desires and apprehensions to an unusual extent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the heroine’s internal life, desires, and perspectives primary—Regency romances often foreground women's viewpoints and emotional experience as the driving force of the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose subgenre approach: traditional vs Regency-set historical
rubrics_metrics.description: As the popularity of the traditional Regency waned, the Regency-set historical stepped up: 'Bolder, sexier, more adventurous, and less restricted, these lively tales kept the trappings of the period but often forfeited much of the traditional sub-genre’s core appeal in order to fit the broader historical mold.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to adhere to the restrictive elegance of traditional Regency (restraint, social consequence, polished wit) or to adopt a broader historical-romance approach (more overt sexuality, adventure, and varied tones)—each choice implies trade-offs in audience expectation and genre conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the period’s cultural moment as an integral backdrop
rubrics_metrics.description: The period’s strange, ephemeral cultural moment is a vital backdrop for the romantic plot: 'From the strict hierarchies to the careful etiquette to the gowns, there’s plenty about the Regency period to keep readers wanting more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat hierarchies, etiquette, fashions, and other social particulars not just as window dressing but as sources of plot tension, character motivation, and thematic resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range of tone and sexual explicitness
rubrics_metrics.description: Regency-set historical romances can range from frothy comedy to suspense to hardcore erotica.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may vary tone and explicitness widely—choose the intended audience and subgenre expectations (comic, suspenseful, erotic, etc.) and adjust language, pacing, and scenes accordingly.
